To record workplace near misses and follow up on corrective actions, a small business can implement a near-miss reporting system. To check whether a new supplier can reliably meet expected order volumes, a small business can review the supplier's past performance data or ask for references. Before committing to large orders, the business may start with a trial order to test the supplier's ability to meet volume and quality requirements on time.

To notify customers and document revised completion dates when a job is delayed, a small business should promptly inform the customer of the delay, explaining the cause and expected impact. The business should agree on a revised completion date with the customer, document the new date and any related changes to the scope or cost, and confirm this in writing to the customer. The business should also update its internal records and project management tools to reflect the revised timeline.

To ensure staff use the current approved version of a form or checklist, a small business can maintain a controlled document list. This list should show the document name, version number, approval date, and distribution. The business should keep obsolete versions separate or clearly marked as superseded, and set a review date for each document. Before releasing a new version, it should communicate the change to relevant staff and provide training if needed.

To document customer-approved changes to a job's scope or price, a small business should require a written change order signed by the customer. The change order should describe the change, its impact on cost and timeline, and any new deliverables or terms. The business should reference the original agreement and note the date and version of the change. It should keep a copy of the signed change order with the job file and update its records accordingly.

To verify that recalled products have been removed from sale, a small business should immediately check stock and sales channels against the recall notice. It should identify and quarantine affected items, remove them from sale, and stop any related marketing or promotions. The business should record the quantities located, actions taken, and confirm with staff that no recalled products remain available for sale. It should also notify customers who may have purchased the recalled product and follow the supplier's instructions for returns or other corrective actions.

To set stock reorder points and avoid both stockouts and excess inventory, a small business can analyze historical sales data to determine average demand and lead times for replenishment. It should set reorder points based on this analysis, considering factors such as supplier lead times, order frequency, and any seasonal fluctuations in demand. The business should also regularly review and adjust reorder points as needed to reflect changes in demand or supply chain conditions.
